There are currently 25 people on death row in Malawi and at least 1300 people at risk of a death sentence including over 50 cases that involve victims with Albinism. Section 176 of the CPEC allows admission of evidence obtained through torture where the court is satisfied beyond reasonable doubt that the confession was made by the accused and that its contents are materially true.

comment.narrative: Malawis death row conditions constitute cruel and inhumane treatment. Almost all death row prisoners are held at Zomba Central Prison in southern Malawi which was condemned in 1997 but is still used today. It is operating at over double its capacity and cells for death row prisoners are roughly 8x6 feet and shared by two to three prisoners. A 2019 report by the Prison Inspectorate found that prisons are dilapidated overcrowded and unfit for human habitation.
Living conditions on the death row at Zomba Central Prison are improved through its eradication or prisoner releases releases to prevent overcrowding and moving people off death row.

No one is serving a sentence on death row. Police prison officers media judges lawyers and paralegals have all been trained on torture and prison conditions. Prison conditions issues were raised with UN Special Rapporteurs the diplomatic community in Malawi and the government of Malawi through communications and clemency applications.

comment.narrative: There are currently 18 legal aid lawyers for a population of 18 million people in Malawi. The system is grossly underfunded and poorly remunerated thus attracting only newly qualified lawyers. Due to limited resources legal aid lawyers currently do not have the resources skills or time to provide highquality investigative legal and advocacy support to those alleging torture and facing a death penalty which conforms to international law standards. Reprieve has already delivered several trainings but due to the complexity of the skillset and the high turnover of Legal Aid staff there is a need for more.
Two best practice guides published on death penalty sentencing and torture.

In Y1 we developed one Civil Society strategy to set out best practice for death penalty abolition. In Y2 we developed a set of best practice submissions on torture for lawyers with accompanying memo on Malawis domestic torture landscape. We also developed a set of guidelines and best practices for judges through the two workshops we held which are captured in a report on the second workshop and accompanying slides.

description.narrative: 2.1. Malawis Constitutional Court considers a strategic legal case challenging s176 of the CP&EC.

comment.narrative: Although torture is prohibited under the Constitution of Malawi there are many reported cases of torture in places of detention especially in police custody and the police are not held accountable. The Police Act of 2010 establishes an Independent Complaints Commission with the mandate to investigate complaints against police officers. However the Commission has not been in operation since it was established in 2010. Evidence obtained through torture is permissible as evidence in court.
Malawis Constitutional Court has consideredbegun considering evidence about the incompatibility of s.176 of the CPEC with the right to freedom from torture.

Malawis High Court judges who sit on the Constitutional Court Supreme Court judges attended two twoday workshops on torture the result of which was agreement of the problems inherent in Section 176 and the need to abolish it to bring the law in line with Malawis constitution. UN SRs sent an urgent letter to the President of Malawi seeking an end to torture as a means to elicit confessions. UN CAT included information and recommendations about s 176 in public report. A strategic case has been identified and will be filed in coming months.

comment.narrative: Some international bodies have already engaged on the prevalence of torture in Malawi as a result of efforts by Reprieve and coapplicants such as the African Court and African Commission. All require continual briefing with uptodate information in order to make informed and strategic interventions.
At least 3 opinions recommendations reports decisions or others by regional and international bodies holding Malawian authorities accountable for breaches of international standards.

10 recommendations including the following In April 2021 four UN SRs sent an urgent letter to the Gov of Malawi recommending urgent action to prohibit torture. In Nov 2022 five UN SRs submitted a communication to the President of Malawi raising the issues of urgent food and water crisis. Our recommendations were also included in reports and concluding observations by UN CAT SR Torture UN ECOSOC and SUMEX. Reports were submitted to inquiries by the CEDAW Committee the ACHPR and various UN bodies. We also attended the ACHPRs inperson session in 2022 participating in the NGO Forum and formal sessions.

In 2007 in Kafantayeni v. Attorney General of Malawi the Malawi High Court struck down the mandatory death penalty as unconstitutional and the Penal Code was amended to reflect this. However the discretionary death penalty remains on the statute books through Section 210 of the Penal Code and is still in use. The death penalty also remains on Malawis statute books through Articles 132 133 301 381 and 309 of Malawis Penal Code. Malawi is currently operating under a de facto moratorium with no executions taking place since 1992 but it has yet to instate a formal official moratorium. The Malawi Resentencing Project helped shift public and influential stakeholder opinion on the death penalty building momentum towards abolition but public angerstatements by the government about devastating violence against people with albinism has led the Malawian authorities to resort to a damaging and false narrative that the death penalty will deter this violence. Government narratives exist that the death penalty is an effective deterrent to crime. description.narrative: 2.3.1. Reports made of violations of human rights related to the use of torture and application of the death penalty to treaty bodies and regional mechanisms including the African Court on Human and Peoples Rights, African Commission, Universal Periodic Review and UN Convention on Torture.

comment.narrative: Some international bodies have already engaged on the prevalence of torture in Malawi as a result of efforts by Reprieve and coapplicants such as African Court and African Commission. All require continual briefing with uptodate information in order to make informed and strategic interventions. Malawis Universal Periodic Review is due to take place in November 2020 Reprieve has made submissions on the death penalty ahead of the session. The African Commission has a review cycle for each state of the Commission Malawis is due to take place this year. They presented a state report and Reprieve submitted a shadow report around the death penalty and torture. CHREAA made a joint stakeholder submission to the UN Committee Against Torture presession review of Malawi in November 2017 at its 62nd session raising concerns regarding lack of comprehensive provisions addressing torture in the Penal Code and also admission of evidence obtained through torture and the lack of investigations where allegation of torture arise. It also highlighted the overcrowding deprivation of adequate nutrition inadequate treatment for inmates with mental illness and general lack of accountability by the state to educate public officials regarding prohibition against torture and to hold them accountable where a breach has been committed.

On 30 occasions international andor regional mechanisms received public briefings statements or submissions from Reprieve on matters relating to the death penalty. These bodies include the African Commission United Nations Secretary General and 9 Special RapporteursIndependent Experts UN CAT UN ECOSOC and UN CEDAW Committees. 4 SRsIE sent the President of Malawi a joint letter urging him to cease the use of the death penalty and torture and 5 SRs wrote him an urgent letter on the dire prison conditions.

comment.narrative: The Malawi Resentencing Project secured the release of more than 145 people originally sentenced to the mandatory death penalty and helped shift public and influential stakeholder opinion on the death penalty building momentum towards abolition. There are no public opinion surveys on the use of the death penalty but our work in the region tells us that there is very little awareness of the legal system death penalty or use of torture in Malawi. There is a common misconception for example that once a death sentence has been handed down the individual will be executed immediately. There are incidences where families believe their loved ones to be dead but in fact they remain on death row. The Malawi Resentencing Project sought views of traditional leaders. In all 94 of the traditional leaders surveyed said that they did not want the death penalty to continue to be a punishment in Malawi. They said they prefer rehabilitation. Recent analysis from a public opinion survey pilot undertaken by Reprieve demonstrated that while there is high support for the death penalty in cases with victims of Albinism around 80 all other crimes had less than 35 support. The increase in attacks on people with Albinism and the response to apply the death penalty highlight that there is still a commonly held opinion that the death penalty is a deterrent to crime. Malawi has demonstrated its increasing openness to the abolition of the death penalty by changing its vote from abstention to votes in favor of the past two UN General Assembly Resolutions for a moratorium on the use of the death penalty in 2016 and 2018.
NGOs report that traditional leaders and faith leaders are supporting advocacy efforts with political decisionmakers and with their own communities.

comment.narrative: Through our work in the region Reprieve and CHREAA have found that there is very little awareness of the legal system the death penalty or the use of torture in Malawi among many influential stakeholder groups as well as the general public. There is a common misconception for example that once a death sentence has been handed down the individual will be executed immediately. There are incidences where families believe their loved ones to be dead but in fact they remain on death row. There is also a widely held and damaging misconception that the death penalty has a deterrence effect.

title.narrative: 3.3.1. Stories pitched to journalists and media outlets (local and international) on individual cases (where appropriate), wider trends, and events to generate press coverage that informs on injustices in the use of torture and application of the death penalty.

description.narrative: 3.3.1. Stories pitched to journalists and media outlets (local and international) on individual cases (where appropriate), wider trends, and events to generate press coverage that informs on injustices in the use of torture and application of the death penalty.

comment.narrative: Journalists currently lack accurate data and analysis as well as compelling human stories and narratives on the use of torture and the death penalty in Malawi and as such these narratives are not shared and disseminated. In Malawi stories can be placed in the media in return for payment. Reprieve and coapplicants have built relationships with journalists that are willing to cover human rights issues in Malawi but require new cases events to cover angles and data as well as compelling human interest stories to pitch relevant and engaging coverage. For a number of years CHREAA has been commemorating the day against torture in prisons where a number of stakeholders were invited to hear testimonies from the prisoners. The UN provided campaign materials in support. In 2019 the EU funded and attended an event by Reprieve and partners on World Day Against the Death Penalty on 10th October at Zomba Central Prison looking at Unseen Victims with a focus on children and families of those sentenced to death.
At least 15 stories pitchedpress releases to a range of media outletsjournalists per year both international and local c. 78 per year.

At least 50 media stories were published on the problems with the death penalty and torture in Malawi via newspaper radio and television pieces. These include 11 episodes of radio drama that was released about which listeners were engaged via social media print media pieces and OpEds by allies about MPs supporting abolition terrible prison conditions the need for the Prisons Bill. Also in Y2 the BBC aired a documentary about wrongful conviction of someone sentenced to death on the Podcast the Comb. There was extensive coverage in the print radio and tv media of the Public Consultations World Day Against the Death Penalty and the National Consultative Conference.

description.narrative: 1. Reduced reports of incidents of torture and other cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment as a result of increased accountability for its use and improved legal standards.

comment.narrative: The use of torture is extensive within Malawis criminal justice system. Over the past three years the police have unlawfully killed over 48 individuals suspected or convicted of committing serious offences such as murder and armed robbery. There have also been deaths in police custody due to harsh and lifethreatening conditions in detention centres. In the same period the media reported that over 43 suspects had died at the hands of the police and that about 70 suspicious deaths have occurred without inquest hearings being conducted. A report from the UN Special Rapporteur on Prisons and Conditions of Detention in Africa documented reports of prisoners being beaten with bottles sticks or burglar bars during interrogation and forced to sign confessions. At a Lilongwe police station the UN delegation found that 17 out of the 43 men detained complained about forced confessions and beatings during interrogation. Evidence obtained through torture is admissible as evidence in courts s176 Criminal Evidence and Procedure Code. There are currently 25 people on death row in Malawi and at least 1300 people are currently at risk of a death sentence including over 50 cases involve victims with Albinism. The death penalty is an available sentence for homiciderelated crimes through articles 210 132 133 301 381 and 309 of Malawis Penal Code.
Reduced incidence of torture in Malawi.
